[h1]I don't like Xenomorphs. They're coarse and rough, and irritating, and they get everywhere.[/h1]
[b]And sadly, here on the Katanga station and the surface of LV-895, very little is pleasant. Quite the opposite.[/b]

  [b] W[/b]hile Aliens: Fireteam Elite is far from being a movie tie-in, its overwhelming dedication to the cult classic from 1986 probably deserves its separate preface and recommendation. While being indifferent to James Cameron's action masterpiece does not make the purchase pointless, lack of affinity for ALIENS does make this game considerably less recommendable in the current market, but thankfully in terms of fan service, it is at worst- a guilty pleasure, at best- a genuinely good treat.

   [b]I[/b]n its time, and with boundaries of the genre, Aliens vs. Predator 2 still ought to be considered a better title, nonetheless when it comes to attention to detail, dedication, and care about the proper translation of the source material, A:FE has moments where it firmly surpasses what the entire AvP series achieved. From flavor text and descriptions of items, atmospheric lighting, environmental design, sound design and music, to writing and the tone of the entire thing- from start to finish it is a proper homage to the fantasy of being a USMC grunt.
Cold Iron Studios did really solid work here, especially considering this is their debut title! The game balances well on a thin line between respect for the IP and creative liberties involved in making a game of this type, and at no point it feels that team lost the will to make good on the opportunity given to them.
That being said, excitement about the familiar setting, easter eggs and other member berries only get you so far and the game should be evaluated predominantly on how it plays, and... it's really not bad! Ultimately on most fronts, it's kinda a mixed bag, but with the aforementioned affinity for the ALIENS and some indulgence, it ends up being a enjoyable, pleasant enough experience. 

   [b]S[/b]o, what is under the hood? Well, a very basic AI companions with zero customizability and borderline nonexistent control over them during missions, that become very insufficient for difficulty levels above medium.
A lot of repetitiveness with barely any additional layers of randomness spicing up replaying campaigns. And even during the first playthrough, the vast majority of activities are a variation of defending against waves of enemies, sometimes interrupted by pressing a button here and there.
And hey- it is the name of the game (genre) but there's artistry in hiding turning gears, distracting players from the barebone formula of progression through linear levels, and fighting off swarm enemies. 
More of that could be forgiven some years ago, but now enough of them passed since Left 4 Dead, to realistically expect a bit more from the core gameplay loop.
It's certainly an issue when taking into account the actual length and construction of the story content, divided into 4 campaigns (chapters) with three missions each, with an additional campaign in Pathogen DLC. All missions are extremely linear, with a handful of extra dead-end corridors and rooms here and there and with scripted set pieces and basic outbursts of enemies along the way. Honestly, the most notable alterations are NPC dialogue lines and responses, that in a few spots in each mission are picked at random.
And this aspect, especially for people playing solo and not using A:FE as a community vehicle to chat with friends, is the weakest pillar of this game.
But probably doesn't deserve equal amount criticism- it doesn't feel like devs ran out of time and money and cut the content short. Quality and polish are there from start to finish without any noticeable drops. That's just what could've been achieved with the resources they had to work with. 

  [b]I[/b]n practice, in the long run, the gameplay is carried by the setting and a few layers of progression and customization- just like in the Killing Floor series, players can play as one of seven classes sharing two out of four weapon groups: pistols, CQW, rifles, and heavy weapons, having a backup pistol, and a couple of special abilities, that can substantially be altered and modified with the perk customization system (fully unlocked after leveling a class to lvl8). The actual perks and modifiers are granted while leveling, as rewards for completing missions, and are found inside special caches (one per mission run), alongside consumables, skins, or emotes. 
A similar source of player income and gear are challenges that come in two types- daily and weekly quests set automatically by the game, and challenges from cards, that can be used during a mission deployment (one per player, using them and deploying destroys the copy of that challenge card), and can be bought in the armory on spaceship Endeavor (player hub) or found in said special caches. Challenge cards offer varying rewards of XP and currency, sometimes none and just provide advantages for those who are struggling. In practice- very simple and rather flexible system.
Plus on top of that- there's player profile leveling, granting cosmetic items every 10 levels of prestige, up to lvl100. Overall not a bad depth considering the amount of actual story/mission content and that, gathering and leveling stuff, is mostly the actual endgame in this genre.

   [b]N[/b]eedless to say, when evaluating A:FE as a product- not a lot of complaints can be directed toward technical performance. After numerous updates, the game is very stable and runs smoothly and reliably from start to finish. The scope and size of the whole thing is rather limited, but never presented deceptively, and in the end, it is overall definitely a case of 'sum bigger than its parts'.
Even with disinterest for the license, Fireteam Elite still might end up a recommendation as long as one knows the limitations of the scope and size of this game. Yes, there are more potent horde shooter or narrative coop experiences, but it is a neat package, that can exist as a pallet cleanser between jumping into heavier games, or as a companion to those. There's very little in terms of systemic or mechanical overhead, which positions this game in a very nice spot where it can permanently sit on a hard drive for occasional dips, without a need to relearn complex systems and familiarize yourself with the flow again. As long as you have friends to play with or the player base remains workable, of course.

   [b]F[/b]or ALIENS fans- it's a no-brainer. Even with a developed allergy to this genre, the entire game can be completed solo on lower difficulties, without the need for an additional human player. On its own, for at least one playthrough, it's more than serviceable, and from start to finish mired in love for the second installment in the Alien cinematic saga.
Do not expect the ability to experience and checkbox everything this game has to offer while playing solo. In the end, the point of playing it becomes sharing the experience with other people while attempting to complete missions on the highest difficulties (and to be fair-split between the story campaign and a few additional modes, cool variations of horde point defense), leveling your player profile and weapons, and completing your perk selection, armaments, and a wide array of cosmetics. And no amount of your persistency can power through basic and lacking AI companions...

   [b]I[/b]f that's not an attractive perspective- just grab it on deep sale and expect to breeze through it and say goodbye after a few hours.
Otherwise- prepare for countless combat drops and a massive mountain of Xenos to climb onto.
